name: Egusi soup
subtitle: A rich, textured soup thickened with ground white melon seeds, leafy greens, crayfish and assorted meats, eaten across Nigeria with pounded yam.

facts.label: Key ingredient
facts.value: Ground egusi (seeds of wild white-seed melon, Citrullus mucosospermus)

facts.label: Traditional swallow
facts.value: Pounded yam, eba (cassava garri), or amala

parts.text: Egusi soup is arguably the most universal celebratory dish in Nigeria, prepared across Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, and Edo households.

It is made from shelled, finely ground melon seeds that form tender, curd-like lumps resembling scrambled eggs when simmered in a seasoned broth with red palm oil, ground dried crayfish, and leafy greens such as bitterleaf, ugwu (fluted pumpkin leaves), or spinach.
The seeds provide natural thickness, a nutty aroma, and an abundance of protein and essential fatty acids, making it a complete nutritional powerhouse.

Egusi soup is rarely eaten on its own; it is served piping hot alongside a large mound of 'swallow' — most prestigiously freshly pounded yam (iyan), but also eba (fried cassava flour stirred with boiling water), fufu, or amala.

Diners use the fingers of their right hand to pinch a small portion of swallow, depress it with the thumb to create a scoop, capture a generous mouthful of egusi soup and leafy greens, and swallow it smoothly.
Unlike cassava, maize, or tomatoes — which were introduced from the Americas during the Atlantic trade — the egusi melon is entirely native to West and Central Africa.
Indigenous communities cultivated the bitter gourd for thousands of years not for its bitter, inedible flesh, but specifically to harvest and dry the oil-rich seeds inside.

blocks.title: Nigerian Egusi Soup (Fried Method)
blocks.sub: Classic fried method recorded by Flo Madubike of All Nigerian Recipes and BBC Good Food.
blocks.note: Spinach or collard greens can substitute for fluted pumpkin leaves (ugwu); unrefined red palm oil provides the authentic color and earthy flavor.

ingredients.name: beef chuck or goat meat, cubed and boiled with stock
dry smoked catfish or stockfish, deboned and flaked
red bell peppers and Scotch bonnet chillies, blended smooth
fresh spinach or chopped ugwu leaves, washed and sliced
rich meat stock (from boiling the beef)

steps.text: Mix the ground egusi in a bowl with a little warm water to form a thick, paste-like dough.
Heat red palm oil in a large pot over medium heat until translucent; add diced onions and sauté until fragrant.
Add the blended pepper and chilli mixture, frying for 8 minutes until the oil separates from the puree.
Scoop small balls of the egusi paste into the hot oil with a spoon; allow them to set without stirring for 5 minutes so they form distinct curds.
Gently stir the curds, pour in the rich meat stock, add the cooked beef, smoked fish, and ground crayfish, and simmer gently.
Fold in the fresh chopped spinach or ugwu leaves, simmering for 3 minutes just until wilted but vibrant green.
Turn off the heat and allow the soup to settle for 5 minutes before serving with hot pounded yam or eba.

gaps: Regional disputes between the Yoruba 'frying' method (oil-fried melon balls) and the eastern Igbo 'caking' or boiling method (ofe egusi) in terms of digestive lightness and taste.
Lack of industrial standardization in local markets where pumpkin seeds or watermelon seeds are occasionally blended into egusi flour.
